comments.text: Optical clarity in fresh water. There is a lake in NZ that is clear out to 70 meters. Similar to distilled water. With that in mind 35 metres seems underwhelming.

replies.author: @davidrobertson-r3i

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Good catch. The 35 metre figure for Pingualuit is a Secchi-disk measurement, while the New Zealand Blue Lake figures are usually based on horizontal underwater visibility, so they aren’t quite the same measurement. But you’re right that Blue Lake has recorded around 70 to 80 metres. I should have said Pingualuit is one of the clearest freshwater lakes in the world rather than implying 35 metres was near the absolute limit. Thanks for pointing it out.

comments.author: @davidk7544
comments.text: It's still simple. Suspicious? It's generally not the *bottom* of a crater that gets ground down, but the rim. The most northern portions of the glacier were not nearly as thick as the southern reaches. Those areas also move less.  The rim is *still* breccia, so obviously the glacier did *not* scrape it dramatically.  This kind of evidence is what testifies to exactly what glaciers did, so this is how we know about glacier behaviour.   I'd have to argue with the federales concluding the water in the crater is "some of the purest". If it's rain water, it's full of formaldehyde, mercury, PFAs, PCBs etc. Do not drink it, or glacial water either. Appearing "clear" is NOT a sign of purity.  Low salinity is expected and means nothing.  High visibility means it's not full of clays and algaes, and not a lot of nitrates there "DIE-uhtoms".  Believe me, science did NOT limit themselves to pollen and diatoms. It's true that people did use to argue a lot about craters being volcanic vs. impact.  Now that we have Gene Shoemaker to reference, it's all clear.   Thanks Gene!  The breccia "reverse folding" is what identifies this as an impact crater. That and the lack of any lava or cinder.  Shocked quartz is the ultimate fingerprint.  Who found this crater is obvious.  Ancient natives.  Whities only ever "rediscover" things, things that were already known for millennia to the locals.  The impact object will *never* be in the center of the crater. It is fragmented into tiny pieces and sprayed all around in the ejecta. This is widely known to be the case. Nobody with any education knows this.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text:
You’ve got a few good points here. Clear water definitely doesn’t mean chemically contaminant-free, researchers have actually measured mercury and perfluorinated compounds in Pingualuit, largely from atmospheric deposition. “Pure” here is really about how exceptionally low the dissolved material and nutrient load are, not literally zero contaminants.

One thing I’d push back on is the ice thickness. Pingualuit was close to former ice-sheet centres/divides, where the ice could actually be very thick but the surface slope and ice flow were relatively low. Researchers also think the crater’s deep geometry may have allowed a subglacial lake to persist and protect the bottom sediments.

And yes, shocked quartz is one of the strongest fingerprints of impact. Breccia by itself isn’t enough, which is why the shock features and impact-melt geochemistry were so important in finally settling the argument. And absolutely, Inuit knew the place long before the aerial “rediscovery.” Appreciate the detailed comment. 👍

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Interesting idea, but in this case the impact explanation is backed by actual physical evidence in the rock, shocked quartz, impact melt, and a meteoritic chemical signature. That’s much stronger than just the crater’s shape. I haven’t seen any credible geological evidence for an electrical discharge or ancient weapon explanation, so I’d stick with the impact interpretation unless something new turns up.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: You actually caught something important there. I went back and checked the research, and Pingualuit was indeed close to former centers of the ice sheet, where the ice was extremely thick but movement was relatively low. So that probably did help explain why the crater survived so well. There was still some documented ice flow across the area, though, so the crater’s depth, shape and possible subglacial lake also seem to have played a role. Good catch, I probably should have emphasized the ice-sheet-center part more in the video. 👍

replies.text: Yeah, the slow ice movement near the old ice-sheet centre seems to be a big part of the story, along with the crater’s deep shape and resistant bedrock. One small thing I’d change though: the round shape doesn’t necessarily mean the meteorite hit at exactly 90 degrees. replies.text: ​@HiddenCanadayeah it's a micro ecology we would want to preserve in its uniqueness and pristine condition for generations of study in a wide array of studies beyond the scope of ecological reasonings.  ❤

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Probably not in the same way. Pingualuit already has native microscopic algae and diatoms, but deliberately adding new algae or nutrients could disrupt an extremely nutrient-poor, isolated ecosystem. That’s part of what makes the lake so scientifically valuable in the first place, researchers generally want to study it without changing it.
